question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
answer:
Counterspell resolves first, and Divination does not resolve at all -- it gets countered.

When all players pass priority in succession, the topmost object on the stack resolves (rule 608.1). Since Counterspell is on top of the stack, it resolves before Divination gets a chance to. As part of Counterspell's resolution, it checks that its target (Divination) is still a legal target (rule 608.2b); assuming Divination hasn't left the stack or become illegal to target, Counterspell's effect applies: "Counter target spell" (per Counterspell's printed text).

To counter a spell means to cancel it, removing it from the stack -- it doesn't resolve and none of its effects occur (rule 701.6a). So Divination never resolves, never draws any cards, and is instead put directly into its owner's graveyard as a countered spell (rule 701.6a). Divination simply sits on the stack beneath Counterspell until Counterspell resolves and removes it (rule 112.1, spell remains on the stack until it resolves or is countered). Note also that no costs paid for Divination are refunded (rule 701.6b), though Divination is a sorcery with no additional costs here.

This assumes the normal order of events: Counterspell was cast in response to Divination and is sitting on top of it, which is the situation you described. If instead Divination had already resolved before Counterspell was cast, Counterspell would have no legal target and would simply fail to resolve, with Divination's cards already drawn -- but that's not the case here.

question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
answer:
You must assign at least 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk (lethal damage equal to its toughness) before any of Charging Rhino's remaining damage can trample over to the defending player -- Vampire Nighthawk's own deathtouch does not lower this requirement. Since Charging Rhino is a 4/4 and has no deathtouch itself, only 1 damage would be left to assign to the defending player.

question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
answer:
Prowess resolves before that cascaded spell. Monastery Swiftspear's prowess is a triggered ability that fires "whenever you cast a noncreature spell" [702.108a]. When Shardless Agent's cascade ability resolves and you choose to cast the exiled nonland card, that casting happens during the resolution of the cascade ability itself, following the steps of 601.2a–i, "except no player receives priority after it's cast" [608.2g]. The cast spell becomes the topmost object on the stack while the cascade ability keeps resolving [608.2g]. Casting a spell is the trigger event for prowess, and any ability that triggers when a spell is cast triggers at that moment [601.2i], but because no priority is given right then, the prowess trigger can't be put on the stack immediately - it waits, the same way any ability whose trigger condition occurs mid-resolution waits and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [704.4, illustrating this timing principle]. Once the cascade ability finishes resolving, the cascaded spell is now the topmost object on the stack, and that's when players next receive priority - at that point the pending prowess trigger is put on the stack on top of everything else, i.e., on top of the cascaded spell, exactly as Monastery Swiftspear normally works: 'Prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger. It will resolve before that spell' [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]. So Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger resolves *before* the cascaded spell resolves, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 first. Note also that prowess isn't tied to the fate of that spell - if the cascaded spell is later countered, the already-triggered prowess still resolves normally [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #3]. Separately, casting Shardless Agent itself (an artifact creature spell) does not trigger prowess, since it has the creature type [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1], and cascade itself simply triggers when you cast Shardless Agent and resolves before Shardless Agent [702.85a; Shardless Agent ruling #1].

question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
answer:
Yes. If Grizzly Bears (a 2/2 creature) already has 2 damage marked on it, it already has lethal damage (damage marked ≥ toughness), and state‑based actions will destroy it the very next time any player would receive priority — which happens *before* your Lightning Bolt gets the chance to resolve.

Here's why: state-based actions are checked every time a player would receive priority (rule [704.3], [117.5]), and this check happens before a player is even allowed to cast a spell such as Lightning Bolt (rule [117.1] requires priority to cast a spell). Rule [704.5g] specifically states that a creature with toughness greater than 0 that has damage marked on it totaling at least its toughness is destroyed as a state-based action; Grizzly Bears' toughness is 2, and 2 damage is already marked on it, so this condition is already met. Regeneration is the only thing that could replace that destruction, and nothing here regenerates it.

So, assuming the 2 damage was already marked on Grizzly Bears before you cast Lightning Bolt (or before Lightning Bolt would resolve), the state-based action destroying Grizzly Bears happens first, at the next priority check, before Lightning Bolt ever resolves. This is consistent with rule [120.5] and [302.7]/[120.6], which clarify that damage itself doesn't destroy a creature — it's the state-based action, checked at the next opportunity, that does.

Timing caveat: this assumes the 2 damage was marked on Grizzly Bears in a separate event/resolution that already finished *before* Lightning Bolt is cast or before it's next in line to resolve. If instead the 2 damage were somehow marked in the middle of the very same resolution as Lightning Bolt itself (which isn't how a simple Lightning Bolt works, since it only deals its own 3 damage), rule [704.4] says state-based actions ignore what happens mid-resolution and only check after that resolution fully completes — but that scenario doesn't apply to a plain Lightning Bolt cast as a separate spell. Also note: since Grizzly Bears would already be destroyed by the state-based action before Lightning Bolt resolves, if Grizzly Bears was Lightning Bolt's only target, Lightning Bolt would have no legal target left and simply not resolve/deal its damage (it's countered by game rules for having no legal targets, per the targeting/priority framework these rules describe, though the specific 'no legal targets' rule text wasn't included here).

question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
answer:
Both triggers happen at the exact same moment — the instant your upkeep step begins — and the order they're stacked in is fixed by the APNAP rule, not by either player's free choice of ordering between the two triggers.

Timing: Under rule [603.2b] and [500.6], a triggered ability with a "beginning of upkeep" trigger condition triggers the instant the upkeep step begins. It doesn't do anything yet at that instant — it's just noted as having triggered. Per [500.6] and [603.3b], any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which per [503.1]/[503.1a] is when the active player (you, since it's your upkeep) is about to receive priority for that step.

Order: Since your Phyrexian Arena's trigger and your opponent's trigger both triggered at the same time (the beginning of your upkeep), rule [603.3b] and rule [101.4] (the APNAP — Active Player, Nonactive Player — ordering rule) govern how they're placed on the stack: you, as the active player, put the triggered abilities you control (Phyrexian Arena's trigger) onto the stack first, choosing their relative order if you control more than one (you only have one here). Then your opponent, as the nonactive player, puts the triggered ability they control onto the stack. Because the ability placed on the stack later ends up on top, your opponent's trigger will be on top of the stack and will resolve first, and Phyrexian Arena's trigger (draw a card, lose 1 life, per its printed text) resolves second. Only after both are on the stack do you, the active player, actually receive priority [503.1a].

Note on player count: This description (single active player, single nonactive player) is the two-player case. If this were a multiplayer game, rule [101.4] still applies but continues past one nonactive player: after you (the active player) place your triggered ability, each remaining nonactive player, in turn order, places their own triggered abilities on the stack — rule [805.7] describes the analogous process for team/multiplayer variants where teams put their triggered abilities on the stack in turn order.

question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
answer:
Only one card ends up back in your hand — the original sorcery card. Fork's copy does not return anything.

Here's why: Buyback (rule [702.27a]) is a static ability that says "if the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner's hand instead of into that player's graveyard as it resolves." That instruction applies to the original sorcery spell — which is a card on the stack (rule [112.1a]) — so when it resolves, that physical card is moved to your hand instead of your graveyard.

When you cast Fork targeting that sorcery, Fork's resolution creates a copy of the sorcery spell and puts it on the stack (rule [707.10]/[707.10b]). This copy copies the sorcery's characteristics and the decisions made for it, including any additional costs paid — so the copy is also considered to have had buyback paid. However, a copy of a spell "is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it" (rules [707.10], [112.1a]). Fork's own ruling confirms this directly: "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you" (Fork ruling #8), and "There is no card representing the copy on the stack" (Fork ruling #10).

So when the copy tries to resolve and its buyback ability tries to put "this spell" into your hand, there's no physical card to move — the copy simply ceases to exist once it leaves the stack, per the state-based action in rule [704.5e] ("If a copy of a spell is in a zone other than the stack, it ceases to exist"). It never actually reaches your hand as a card.

Net result: after both the original buyback sorcery and Fork's copy have resolved, exactly one physical card (the original sorcery) is in your hand, not two.

question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
answer:
No, you don't get a token. Lightning Bolt is an instant card, not a permanent card, and the activated ability of Mimic Vat can only create a token copy of an exiled permanent card. As Mimic Vat's own ruling states, if the creature that died was actually an instant or sorcery card that had been manifested, Mimic Vat may end up with a nonpermanent card exiled, and you can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card — so no token is created in that case.

Here's why this happens even though the imprint trigger let you exile it: manifesting turns a face-down permanent that's secretly Lightning Bolt, but the card's real characteristics (instant) are what matter once it's revealed. When the manifested permanent died, its printed characteristics as an instant card are exiled with Mimic Vat via its Imprint ability. When you later activate Mimic Vat's second ability, 'Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact,' the game checks the exiled card's characteristics — an instant card can't be copied into a permanent token, so the ability simply fizzles with no token created, exactly as described for this scenario.

Note that this differs from the case where nothing was ever exiled at all (rule 111.12, where there's no object at all to copy) — here there IS an exiled card, it's just not a permanent, which is why the ruling specifically calls out that no token results.

question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
answer:
Yes — both exiled creatures return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Fiend Hunter's second ability ("When this creature leaves the battlefield, return the exiled card to the battlefield under its owner's control") is linked to its first, enters-the-battlefield exile ability (rule 607.1). Per Lithoform Engine's own ruling: "If an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability are also linked to that second ability... if Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability is copied and two creatures are exiled, they both return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield" [Lithoform Engine ruling #4]. So the copy made by Lithoform Engine's {2}, {T} ability remains linked to Fiend Hunter's leaves-the-battlefield trigger, exactly as the original ability is. Since the leaves-the-battlefield ability refers to "the exiled card" and there are now two such cards (one from the original resolution, one from the copy), rule 607.3 confirms that when a linked ability's partner has exiled multiple cards, the ability performing an action on "the" card performs that action on each of them. Assuming both exile events actually happened (i.e., both instances of the enters-the-battlefield ability resolved and successfully exiled their targeted creatures) before Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, both creatures will be returned to the battlefield under their owners' control simultaneously when Fiend Hunter's leaves-the-battlefield ability resolves. If instead Fiend Hunter left the battlefield before one or both exile instances resolved, per Fiend Hunter's own ruling, the leaves-the-battlefield ability would already have triggered and done nothing for that instance, and the still-pending enters-the-battlefield ability would exile its target creature indefinitely rather than returning it [Fiend Hunter ruling #0].

question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
answer:
No. The exiled creature stays exiled; phasing Banishing Light out does not cause it to leave the battlefield, so the "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield" condition is not met.

Banishing Light's triggered ability exiles the target "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." When Teferi's Protection causes Banishing Light to phase out, the rules explicitly treat this as different from leaving the battlefield: phasing doesn't actually move a permanent to a different zone (rule [702.26d]), and Teferi's Protection ruling #21 states directly that one-shot effects waiting "until [this] leaves the battlefield," such as Banishing Light's, won't happen when a permanent phases out. So the creature remains exiled while Banishing Light is phased out.

When Banishing Light later phases back in (during your untap step, per the Teferi's Protection reminder text and rule [502.1]), it's the same object continuously exiling that creature — phasing in/out doesn't trigger leaves- or enters-the-battlefield abilities [702.26d], and Banishing Light rulings #1/#5 confirm the exile only ends if Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield before/while its effect is active. Since it never left the battlefield (it only phased out), the exiled creature does not return.

This holds for both two-player and multiplayer games, since nothing here depends on player count — the phasing rules and the Teferi's Protection ruling apply the same regardless of how many players are at the table.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
answer:
Yes, your opponent's Counterspell can legally target Emrakul, the Promised End while it's still a spell on the stack, and even if it counters Emrakul, you still gain control of the target opponent during their next turn.

Here's why. Emrakul, the Promised End's protection from instants only functions while Emrakul is a permanent on the battlefield — per [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2], "Protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield. Notably, Emrakul may be the target of a spell that targets it while on the stack, such as Syncopate." Counterspell ("Counter target spell") works the same way: it targets Emrakul the spell while it's on the stack, and protection from instants does nothing to prevent that targeting there.

Sequencing matters here too. Emrakul's ability "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn" is a triggered ability that triggers once the casting of Emrakul is complete [601.2i]. Triggered abilities go onto the stack as their own object, separate from any card, the next time a player would receive priority [405.1], [117.2a] — so this trigger sits on the stack *above* the Emrakul spell, targeting your opponent. If your opponent casts Counterspell in response to that trigger, Counterspell ("Counter target spell") can only target the Emrakul spell itself, not the triggered ability — activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells and can't be countered by something that only counters spells [113.9]. Counterspell resolves first (last object put on the stack resolves first) and counters Emrakul, sending the card to the graveyard. But the triggered ability is an independent object already on the stack; nothing about countering the spell removes it. It then resolves on its own, giving you control of the targeted opponent during that player's next turn, and per Emrakul's own text, an extra turn follows for that opponent after that turn.

So: your opponent's Counterspell is a legal target of the Emrakul spell (protection doesn't block it there), and even a successful counter of Emrakul does not stop the "gain control of target opponent" trigger from resolving, since that trigger is already a separate object on the stack by the time Counterspell could be cast in response to it.

question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
answer:
This is a legal cascade hit, but casting it for free will give you Valki, God of Lies on the front face — not Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor.

First, the hit: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card whose mana value (per the card data) is 2 while it's anywhere other than the stack, including while it sits in exile as a cascade-exiled card. Cascade [702.85a] requires you to exile cards "until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than this spell's mana value." Since Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has mana value 2 in exile, it's a legal card to stop on as long as your cascading spell's mana value is greater than 2.

Second, casting it for free: cascade [702.85a] lets you "cast that card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell's mana value is less than this spell's mana value." Casting doesn't, by itself, give you permission to put the back face (Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor) on the stack. Rule [712.11c] says a double-faced spell is cast with its front face up by default, and only that front face is evaluated for legality and put onto the stack. Rule [712.11d] carves out an exception only when "an ability of a double-faced card's front face allows it to be cast 'transformed' or 'converted'" — Valki, God of Lies has no such ability, and cascade itself grants no such permission either. So the cascade trigger can only let you cast the front face, Valki, God of Lies, for free — its mana value as cast would be 2 (from its mana cost {1}{B}), which needs to be less than your cascading spell's mana value (the same threshold that let you stop on it in the first place, so this is automatically satisfied). You cannot use cascade to cast the back face, Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, at all, transformed or otherwise, since nothing here grants that permission (see also [712.8c] on how a nonmodal/modal DFC's face-up status on the stack depends on such explicit permission).

If instead you had an effect that specifically let you cast this card "transformed" or "converted" as part of the cascade-triggered cast, that would change things — but plain cascade does not include that language.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
You end up controlling exactly one of your opponent's turns, but that opponent will take two extra turns; and yes, you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End (as a token), but that token does NOT give you another "gain control of a turn" trigger.

Here's the play-by-play. After you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its triggered ability ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.") goes on the stack above the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself, which is still sitting on the stack unresolved [112.1a][601.2a]. You use Lithoform Engine's first ability to copy that triggered ability [707.10][707.10b]; the copy is put on the stack on top of the existing stack, so it sits above the original trigger. After untapping Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key, you use Lithoform Engine's third ability to copy the still-unresolved Emrakul, the Promised End spell (a permanent spell); this creates a copy of the spell on the stack, on top of everything else [Lithoform Engine ruling #5]. That copy is itself a spell, but per rule 707.10 "a copy of a spell isn't cast," and Lithoform Engine's own ruling confirms this directly: "The copy is created on the stack, so it's not 'cast'... Creating the copy won't cause abilities that trigger when a player casts a spell...to trigger" [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. Since Emrakul, the Promised End's ability only triggers "when you cast this spell," and this copy is never cast, no third control trigger is generated. So: no extra control trigger from copying the spell.

When that spell-copy resolves, rule 111.13 says "A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. The token has the characteristics of the spell that became that token." So you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a 13/13 flying, trample, protection-from-instants token on the battlefield [111.13].

Next, the two triggered-ability instances resolve in turn: the copy created by Lithoform Engine resolves first (it's on top), then the original triggered ability resolves. Each instance independently says "you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." Since both target the same opponent's same upcoming "next turn," Emrakul, the Promised End's own ruling controls the outcome: "Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works... each ability's effect will create an extra turn" [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. That means only one control effect actually takes hold on that single next turn (the one created later overwrites the earlier one) — you control exactly one turn, not two — but because each instance still independently creates its own delayed "after that turn, take an extra turn" trigger, both extra-turn triggers still resolve, giving your opponent two extra turns after the one turn you controlled. Those two extra turns are normal turns under your opponent's own control; nothing in the ability text gives you control of the extra turns themselves.

Assumption note: I'm assuming a two-player game with a single opponent, so both triggered-ability instances target the same player and thus conflict per ruling #14. In a multiplayer game, if you instead chose new targets so the Lithoform Engine copy targeted a different opponent, you would control one turn from each of the two different opponents (no overwrite, since ruling #14's overwrite only applies when effects affect "the same player"), and each opponent would separately get one extra turn afterward, per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #17's multiplayer framing. I'm also assuming the copied triggered ability resolves before the original trigger (since it's created and stacked on top later); if the order were reversed, the same overwrite math (one turn controlled, two extra turns) would still apply, just with the other instance being the one that "wins" the control effect.

question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
answer:
Yes — you'll get two token copies of the imprinted creature card, each with haste, each set to be exiled at the beginning of the next end step. When Lithoform Engine's first ability ("Copy target activated or triggered ability you control") resolves, it puts a copy of Mimic Vat's activated ability onto the stack [707.10b]. question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
Casting Awaken the Woods with X=0 costs {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total: 1 generic, 2 green) and nets you zero Forest Dryad tokens — a complete waste of mana. You should instead choose X=2, which costs the exact same total, {1}{G}{G}, but gives you 2 Forest Dryad tokens.

Here's why. Awaken the Woods' mana cost is {X}{G}{G}. Per rule 601.2f, you first determine the mana cost with X filled in, then apply cost increases/reductions in the order that produces the 'total cost,' which then locks in.

With X=0, the mana cost is {0}{G}{G}, i.e. just {G}{G} (2 mana, no generic component at all). Your permanent's 'costs {1} less' effect only reduces the generic mana component of a cost (rule 118.7a: 'Effects that reduce a cost by an amount of generic mana affect only the generic mana component of that cost. They can't affect the colored or colorless mana components.'). Since {G}{G} has no generic mana to reduce, your reducer does nothing here. That leaves a 2-mana cost, which is less than three mana, so Trinisphere's static ability (as printed on Trinisphere: 'each spell that would cost less than three mana to cast costs three mana to cast... additional mana in the cost may be paid with any color of mana or colorless mana') bumps it up by adding {1} generic, giving a final total cost of {1}{G}{G} (3 mana) for zero tokens — Trinisphere ruling #0 confirms you apply reductions first, then check Trinisphere's threshold last, before the total cost locks in.

If you instead choose X=2, the mana cost is {2}{G}{G}. Now your {1}-generic reduction has a generic component to bite into (rule 118.7a again), reducing it to {1}{G}{G} — which is already 3 mana, so Trinisphere's 'less than three mana' clause no longer applies and doesn't add anything more. Final total cost: {1}{G}{G} (3 mana: 1 generic, 2 green) — identical to the X=0 cost, but now you get 2 Forest Dryad tokens instead of 0.

Going higher than X=2 only raises your total cost further (e.g., X=3 costs {2}{G}{G}, 4 mana), so X=2 is the efficient sweet spot given this specific Trinisphere/reducer combination — you're getting the extra token 'for free' because the {1} reduction and Trinisphere's 3-mana floor cancel out at exactly X=2. This analysis assumes you control only the one {1}-less reducer and no other cost effects, and that Trinisphere remains untapped throughout the casting process (per Trinisphere ruling #1, if Trinisphere left the battlefield or changed tap state as part of paying this spell's cost, that would be resolved only after the total cost is already locked in, which isn't the case in this scenario).

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes, you can cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard, but the moment it resolves, Grist gets returned to the battlefield and then has to be immediately sacrificed — you don't get to keep it as a planeswalker.

Here's why: Grist, the Hunger Tide's own text says "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types," and its ruling confirms that anywhere but the battlefield (including your graveyard) it's a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect (Grist, the Hunger Tide; [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]). That means while it's sitting in your graveyard, it qualifies as a "creature card in a graveyard," so Animate Dead can legally target it when you cast it, and rule [608.2b] confirms that legality is rechecked (it's still a creature card in a graveyard) as Animate Dead resolves.

When Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield ability resolves, it returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and tries to attach itself, having gained the new enchant text "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura" (Animate Dead). But the instant Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield, its own text means it's no longer a creature — it's just a planeswalker. That makes it illegal for Animate Dead to attach to, since Animate Dead's enchant restriction still requires the object to be a creature. This is exactly the situation covered by [Animate Dead ruling #4]: when the returned card can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead "for another reason," Animate Dead can't attach, and it's put into the graveyard as a state-based action. That triggers Animate Dead's delayed "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability (Animate Dead), which then makes you sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide as soon as that trigger resolves (assuming it's still on the battlefield at that point, which it will be).

Net result: Grist, the Hunger Tide briefly returns to the battlefield as a planeswalker, Animate Dead immediately falls off into your graveyard, and you then have to sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide, sending it back to your graveyard (where, per its own text, it becomes a creature card again since it's off the battlefield). You don't get any lasting use out of Grist, the Hunger Tide's loyalty abilities from this.

This assumes Grist, the Hunger Tide isn't affected by some other continuous effect making it remain a creature while on the battlefield; if some other effect kept it as a creature, Animate Dead would be able to stay attached instead, per the general logic in [Animate Dead ruling #4] (Aura only detaches if the enchanted object truly can't legally be enchanted).

question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
answer:
Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps all four +1/+1 counters through this entire sequence, but Doubling Season does not double them.

Walkthrough: Skullbriar's own printed ability states, "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." This overrides the general rule that counters cease to exist when an object changes zones (rule [122.2]), for any zone change that isn't into a hand or a library.

1. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies, you may use the commander replacement effect to put it into the command zone instead of the graveyard (rule [903.9b]). The command zone is neither a hand nor a library, so Skullbriar's four +1/+1 counters remain on it as it moves there.

2. When you subsequently cast Skullbriar, the Walking Grave from the command zone, the card moves from the command zone to the stack. Again, the stack is not a hand or library, so the counters remain. Rule [400.10] notes that being *put into* the command zone doesn't change zones, but that's irrelevant here since we're now talking about the card *leaving* the command zone to be cast.

3. When the spell resolves and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave enters the battlefield, the battlefield is again neither a hand nor a library, so the four counters remain on it as it enters. Note that Skullbriar's ruling confirms this applies to all counter types, not just +1/+1 counters (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1), and that it works normally in a merged/melded-commander context too via rule [903.9c] if that ever applied (not the case here since Skullbriar isn't merged/melded).

Crucially, because these counters *remain* on Skullbriar rather than being *placed* or *put* on it by an effect, Doubling Season's second ability -- "If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many of those counters on that permanent instead" -- never triggers for them. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2 says this explicitly: "The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones aren't 'placed' on Skullbriar. Effects like Doubling Season's... won't affect those counters." So even with Doubling Season on the battlefield, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters with exactly four +1/+1 counters, not eight.

(If Doubling Season had instead been relevant to counters Skullbriar gained from combat damage triggers after re-entering, those *would* be doubled, since that's a genuine "put a counter" effect -- but that's a separate event from the counters it retains through this zone-change sequence.)

question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
answer:
No, you do not lose the game. Final Fortune's delayed triggered ability says "At the beginning of that turn's end step, you lose the game." This ability can only trigger if the end step actually begins. When you activate Sundial of the Infinite's ability, "End the turn," during that extra turn but before its end step, the game follows the special end-the-turn process in rule [724.1]: the current phase/step ends, all attacking/blocking creatures are removed from combat, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every step in between — including the end step [724.1d]. Because the end step is skipped entirely rather than merely passed through, the "at the beginning of the end step" trigger condition never occurs. Rule [724.1e] states this explicitly: "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities don't trigger because the end step is skipped. This mirrors the ruling on Sundial of the Infinite itself: activating it before the end step means "at the beginning of the end step"-triggered abilities won't get the chance to trigger that turn [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1], and the whole ending process (exiling the stack, removing creatures from combat, checking state-based actions, ending the step/phase, and skipping straight to the cleanup step) happens with no player getting priority and no triggered abilities put on the stack [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4]. Since Final Fortune's lose-the-game ability is a triggered ability tied specifically to the beginning of the end step, and that end step never begins, the ability simply never triggers — you don't lose the game. This is consistent with Final Fortune's own ruling that if the extra turn (or, here, its end step) never actually happens as normal, the loss doesn't occur [Final Fortune ruling #1].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Sundial of the Infinite's ability is activated during the extra turn granted by Final Fortune, at some point before the end step begins (e.g., during a main phase or combat of that turn), which is what the question describes. If instead you activated it during the end step itself (after the end step had already begun), Final Fortune's trigger would have already gone on the stack or already resolved, and ending the turn afterward would not undo an already-triggered or already-resolved loss.

question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
answer:
You choose what Clone copies at the moment Clone enters the battlefield, as part of Clone's "as this creature enters" replacement effect — you do this yourself, since Clone's controller (you) gets to make any "as ... enters the battlefield" choices for it [707.6]. This is not a target, so there's no opportunity for your opponent to respond specifically to that choice: Clone's copying ability doesn't target the chosen creature [Clone ruling #0], and a replacement effect applied as a permanent enters the battlefield isn't a stack action that grants priority — it simply happens as part of Clone becoming a permanent on the battlefield.

Mechanically: while you cast Clone, you go through the normal steps of casting a spell (announcing the spell, paying costs, etc.) under rule 601.2c, but since Clone requires no targets, no target is chosen at that time. Once the Clone spell resolves and Clone is about to enter the battlefield, the replacement effect from its printed text ("You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield") applies, and you choose which permanent already on the battlefield to copy — or you may choose to copy nothing, in which case Clone enters as a 0/0 Shapeshifter (and normally dies immediately as a state-based action) [Clone ruling #5]. Note that you can only pick a creature that is already on the battlefield: if Clone somehow enters at the same time as another creature, you cannot choose that other creature as the thing to copy [Clone ruling #2].

Because this choice is made as part of the permanent entering the battlefield rather than through an activated or triggered ability, your opponent gets no window to respond to the choice itself — there's no priority pass in between "Clone enters" and "the copy choice is made." Your opponent's only real opportunity to interact is earlier, while the Clone spell itself is still on the stack (e.g., casting an instant to remove or otherwise change the available creatures on the battlefield before Clone resolves and the copy choice is made). This answer applies regardless of player count, since nothing here depends on how many opponents there are — the choice is a single replacement-effect choice made by Clone's controller, not a multiplayer-order matter (rule 616.1c's APNAP ordering for copy-effect replacement choices only comes into play if multiple such replacement effects are competing to affect the same object, which isn't the case for a single Clone entering normally).

question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
answer:
You get three lands in the battlefield total (assuming you choose to find a Plains or Island each time) — one from the original Flooded Strand activation and one from each of Gogo, Master of Mimicry's two copies, for three separate searches.

Here's why: Flooded Strand's activated ability reads "{T}, Pay 1 life, Sacrifice this land: Search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle." When you activate Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability with X=2 targeting that activated ability on the stack, it creates two additional copies of that ability on the stack (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6, ruling #8). Copying an ability means putting a copy of it onto the stack — a copy of an activated ability isn't 'activated' again, and it doesn't require you to have another Flooded Strand to sacrifice, since the ability's text just says 'search your library,' not 'search the library of the land that was sacrificed' [707.10]. The source of each copy is still Flooded Strand itself (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9), but the copies exist independently as separate abilities on the stack.

So you now have three instances of the ability on the stack: the original plus two copies. Each one resolves separately, and each resolution is a complete 'search library, put a card onto the battlefield, then shuffle' cycle on its own — this is different from rule [701.23h], which only merges multiple search instructions that belong to a single ability's text before one shuffle. Here you have three distinct abilities, each with its own search-and-shuffle, so they don't merge. Each resolution lets you search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle your library before the next one resolves.

Note that you aren't required to find a card each time — per rule [701.23b], search effects with a stated quality never force you to find a match even if one exists — but if your library still has enough Plains or Island cards and you choose to find one each time, three copies/original resolving means three lands hit the battlefield from that single Flooded Strand activation.

Howling Mine’s controller has another Howling Mine in her graveyard and two more in her library.
